rounds.method_summary: This selector uses farthest-first traversal in the 64-dimensional feature space, weighted by pair uncertainty (highest when logits are near the decision boundary of 0). By combining uncertainty sampling with diversity-promoting selection, we choose informative pairs that are both hard for the current model and represent distinct regions of feature space, improving the reward model's ranking accuracy more than random selection.

This selector uses pivot-based clustering to improve diversity: it samples pivots weighted by uncertainty, assigns each point to its nearest pivot, then selects the highest-quality candidate from each of the top-k pivots, ensuring coverage of distinct feature regions while prioritizing uncertain pairs near the decision boundary. This replaces the sequential greedy farthest-first traversal with a single nearest-pivot assignment, making it more efficient and less prone to myopic local optima.

rounds.method_summary: This selector uses pivot-based clustering with uncertainty-weighted diversity in early rounds (1–9) for broad coverage, then switches to a minimum-cost bipartite matching on the top-5000 quality candidates in later rounds (10–39) to select k pairs that jointly maximize both uncertainty and feature-space diversity through a distance-minus-quality cost function. The round-based schedule balances exploration early with more precise diverse selection once the model has enough signal.

This selector replaces the bipartite matching and cluster-pick strategies with a single efficient greedy facility-location selection across the top-k*40 quality candidates, jointly maximizing uncertainty and minimum feature-distance to already-chosen pairs. Pivot-based uncertainty-weighted sampling still seeds an approximate density/quality score, but final selection uses vectorized argmax over a cached min-distance array for speed and consistency across all rounds 1–39.

rounds.method_summary: This selector unifies all rounds with a single minimum-cost bipartite matching strategy on the top-k*15 quality candidates (quality = uncertainty × exp(-nearest_pivot_dist/sigma)), with cost = 2·distance − average_quality·sigma to balance diversity and informativeness. Removing the early/late round split simplifies the logic and applies matching-based diversity throughout training, while increasing pivots to k*4 improves quality estimate robustness.

This selector increases the quality candidate pool from k*15 to k*20 and uses a round-dependent diversity weight (alpha=3.0 in early rounds 1–9, alpha=2.0 in later rounds 10–39) in the bipartite matching cost function. The higher early-round alpha prioritizes broader feature-space coverage when the model is less reliable, while the lower late-round alpha shifts focus back toward uncertain, high-information pairs as training progresses.

This selector reduces the quality candidate pool from k*15 to k*12 for faster bipartite matching and uses argpartition instead of full sort for efficiency, while adjusting the diversity weight alpha to 2.5 in early rounds (1–9) and 1.8 in later rounds to balance exploration and exploitation better than the previous fixed alpha of 2.0.
